source_text: Omnia autem penes ueritatem dei fixa sunt. ethnici, quos penes nulla est ueritatis plenitudo, quia nec doctor ueritatis deus, malum et bonum pro arbitrio et libidine interpretantur: alibi bonum quod alibi malum, et alibi malum quod alibi bonum. sic ergo euenit, ut qui in publico uix necessitate uesicae tunicam leuet, idem in circo aliter non t exuet, nisi totum pudorem in faciem omnium intendit, ut et qui filiae uirginis ab omni spurco uerbo aures tuetur, ipse eam in theatrum ad illas uoces gesticulationesque deducat, et qui in plateis litem manu agentem aut compescit aut detestatur, idem in stadio grauioribus pugnis suffragium ferat, et qui ad cadauer hominis communi lege defuncti exhorret, idem in amphitheatro derosa et dissipata et in suo sanguine squalentia corpora patientissmis oculis desuper incumbat, immo qui propter homicidaecidae poenam probandam ad spectaculum ueniat, idem gladia torem ad homicidium flagellis et uirgis compellat inuitum, et qui insigniori cuique homicidae leonem poscit, idem gladiatori atroci petat rudem et pilleum praemium conferat, illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetat, libentius recognoscens de proximo quem uoluit occidere de lonquinquo, tanto durior, si non ualuit.
thought_title: Pagans' shifting standards of good and evil
orientation: Tertullian is contrasting the fixed truth of God with the arbitrary moral judgments of pagans, showing how the same people behave inconsistently in public life and at the shows.
pass_a_gloss: But all things are fixed with the truth of God. The pagans, with whom there is no fullness of truth, because God is not their teacher of truth, interpret evil and good according to their own will and desire: in one place good what in another place is evil, and in one place evil what in another place is good. So therefore it happens that he who in public scarcely lifts his tunic because of the necessity of his bladder, the same man in the circus does not strip otherwise, unless he directs all his shame into the face of everyone, and he who guards the ears of his virgin daughter from every filthy word, himself leads her into the theater to those voices and gestures, and he who in the streets either restrains or detests a man acting out a quarrel with his hand, the same man in the stadium gives his vote to more serious fistfights, and he who shudders at the corpse of a man who has died by the common law, the same man in the amphitheater leans over from above with most patient eyes upon bodies torn apart and scattered and filthy in their own blood, indeed he who comes to the show to approve the punishment of a murderer, the same man compels an unwilling gladiator to murder with whips and rods, and he who demands a lion for every more distinguished murderer, the same man asks for the wooden sword and confers the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator, but demands back that man, finished off, even as a spectacle for his face, recognizing more gladly from nearby the man whom he wanted killed from afar, so much the harder, if he did not prevail.

choices.english: are fixed with the truth of God
choices.why: penes means 'in the possession of' or 'with'; the point is that all things have their fixed standard in God's truth
rejected: are fixed by the truth of God

choices.english: according to their own will and desire
choices.why: arbitrium is judgment or will, libido is desire or whim; the pair conveys arbitrary, self-serving moral judgment

choices.term: totum pudorem in faciem omnium intendit
choices.english: directs all his shame into the face of everyone
choices.why: intendit means to direct or aim; the image is of shamelessly exposing himself before all
rejected: casts all modesty in everyone's face

choices.why: suffragium ferre is the standard phrase for casting a vote; here it means approving or cheering the fights

choices.english: leans over from above with most patient eyes
choices.why: incumbo means to lean over or upon; desuper indicates from above, i.e., from the seats; patientissimis oculis is an ablative of manner
rejected: gazes down with most patient eyes
bends over with most enduring eyes

choices.english: confers the wooden sword and the cap as a prize
choices.why: rudis is the wooden sword given to a discharged gladiator, pilleum the cap of freedom; conferat means to bestow or confer
rejected: gives the rod and cap as reward
grants the wooden sword and cap

pass_b_english: But all things are fixed by the truth of God. Pagans possess no fullness of truth, because God is not their teacher of truth. They interpret good and evil according to their own whim and desire: what is good in one place is evil in another, and what is evil in one place is good in another.

So it happens that the same man who in public would barely lift his tunic out of necessity to relieve his bladder, in the circus strips off his clothing only to throw all his shame in the face of everyone. The man who guards his virgin daughter's ears from every obscene word himself leads her into the theater to hear those voices and see those gestures. The man who in the streets either breaks up or detests a brawl carried on by hand, in the stadium gives his vote to more serious fights. The man who shudders at the corpse of a person who died by the common law of nature, in the amphitheater leans over from above with most patient eyes upon bodies torn and scattered, and filthy in their own blood.

Indeed, the man who comes to the show to approve the punishment of a murderer, himself compels an unwilling gladiator to commit murder with whips and rods. And the man who demands a lion for some distinguished murderer, demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator. He also has the slain gladiator brought back so he can look at his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.

problems.quote: demands back that same man, now finished, for the spectacle of his face
problems.source_quote: illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetit
problems.why: Latin says he repeats the spectacle of his face; English says he demands the man back, changing who acts and what is done.
problems.fix: repeats the spectacle of his face, showing the dead man’s visage again

edits.old: and then demands back that same man, now finished, for the spectacle of his face—more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.
edits.new: and then repeats the spectacle of his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.

fixed: Changed 'demands back that same man, now finished, for the spectacle of his face' to 'repeats the spectacle of his face' to match the source 'illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetit', where the subject repeats the spectacle of the face rather than demanding the man back.

problems.quote: the wooden sword and the cap as a prize
problems.why: “rudem” means “raw/unrefined” not “wooden sword”; the translation invents a detail.
problems.fix: the raw weapon and the cap as a prize

problems.quote: and then repeats the spectacle of his face
problems.source_quote: illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetat
problems.why: 'illum' refers to the gladiator just spared, not 'his face'; 'oris spectaculo' is the spectacle of the mouth (kissing).
problems.fix: then demands the exhausted man even for the spectacle of the mouth
problems.ruling: Latin 'oris spectaculo' = spectacle of the mouth (or oral display), not 'his face'; misreading changes meaning.

edits.old: confers the wooden sword and the cap as a prize on a cruel gladiator
edits.new: confers the raw weapon and the cap as a prize on a cruel gladiator

edits.old: and then repeats the spectacle of his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance
edits.new: and then demands back that same man, now finished, even for the spectacle of the mouth, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance

fixed: Corrected 'wooden sword' to 'raw weapon' per source 'rudem' (raw/unrefined), not a wooden sword.

Corrected 'repeats the spectacle of his face' to 'demands back that same man, now finished, even for the spectacle of the mouth' per source 'illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetat' where 'illum' refers to the gladiator and 'oris spectaculo' is the spectacle of the mouth.

problems.quote: even for the spectacle of the mouth
problems.source_quote: illum uero confectum etiam oris spectaculo repetat
problems.why: Phrase "spectacle of the mouth" is not in the Latin; misrenders "oris spectaculo".
problems.fix: even in the spectacle of the mouth

problems.quote: confers the raw weapon and the cap as a prize on a cruel gladiator
problems.source_quote: idem gladiatori atroci petat rudem et pilleum praemium conferat
problems.why: The subject is the same spectator who 'demands' (petat) the rudis and pilleum for the gladiator, not 'confer' them. The spectator petitions for the gladiator's freedom.
problems.fix: demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator
problems.ruling: Latin has "petat ... conferat" (may demand and may confer); English only renders "confers", omitting the demand.

problems.quote: gnawed away, torn apart, and filthy in their own blood
problems.source_quote: derosa et dissipata et in suo sanguine squalentia corpora
problems.why: Adds "gnawed away" not present; source says only torn and scattered.
problems.fix: torn and scattered, and filthy in their own blood
problems.ruling: derosa = 'gnawed away' (from derodere), distinct from dissipata 'torn apart'; both present in source, not an addition.

edits.old: confers the raw weapon and the cap as a prize on a cruel gladiator
edits.new: demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator

edits.old: and then demands back that same man, now finished, even for the spectacle of the mouth
edits.new: and then demands back that same man, now finished, even as a spectacle for his face

edits.old: upon bodies gnawed away, torn apart, and filthy in their own blood
edits.new: upon bodies torn and scattered, and filthy in their own blood

fixed: The English 'confers the raw weapon and the cap as a prize on a cruel gladiator' misstates the source 'idem gladiatori atroci petat rudem et pilleum praemium conferat': the verb is 'petat' (demands), not 'conferat' (confers). The spectator demands the rudis and pilleum for the gladiator. Fixed to 'demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator'.
The English 'even for the spectacle of the mouth' misrenders 'etiam oris spectaculo': 'oris' here means 'of his face', not 'of the mouth'. Fixed to 'even as a spectacle for his face'.

The English 'gnawed away, torn apart, and filthy in their own blood' adds 'gnawed away' not present in the source 'derosa et dissipata et in suo sanguine squalentia corpora'. Fixed to 'torn and scattered, and filthy in their own blood'.

fixed.quote: and then demands back that same man, now finished, even as a spectacle for his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.
fixed.fix: and has the other one, the man who was finished off, brought back so he can look at his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.
fixed.note: 'illum' is the other, beaten gladiator, not 'that same man', and 'oris spectaculo' means to look at his face; the checker's 'repeats the spectacle' is also wrong.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening statement about God's truth, smoothed the long sentence about the man in the circus, and broke the dense final passage into clearer paragraphs while preserving every claim and image.

notes.quote: the wooden sword and the cap as a prize
notes.why: Symbols of a gladiator's discharge; reader cannot know their meaning.
notes.fix: Gloss: 'the wooden sword and the cap (symbols of a gladiator's freedom)'

polish.changed: Broke the long final sentence into two sentences, clarified that the same man demands both the lion and the gladiator's prize, and replaced the ambiguous 'the other one, the man who was finished off' with 'the slain gladiator' so the reader can follow who is being brought back.

notes.quote: the man who demands a lion for some distinguished murderer, demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator, and has the other one, the man who was finished off, brought back so he can look at his face
notes.why: Complex sentence with multiple 'demands'; reader loses track of who demands what and who 'the other one' is.
notes.fix: Break into shorter sentences with clear subjects.

notes.quote: has the other one, the man who was finished off, brought back so he can look at his face
notes.why: 'Finished off' is ambiguous: it could mean killed or defeated; the Latin likely refers to a slain gladiator.
notes.fix: Read 'the man who was killed' or 'the man who was slain.'
